At the moment of eclosion, the newly released glochidia measure just 0.02 cm [Lb = 0.02 cm] in shell length, a diminutive size typical of freshwater mussels with a parasitic larval phase. Following a short free-swimming period, the veliger larva undergoes settlement and metamorphosis, during which the shell length at settlement reaches about 0.03 cm . This transition marks the onset of the post-metamorphic juvenile stage, when the young mussel begins to establish itself on the substrate. The prodissoconch stage is brief, and the growing juvenile rapidly increases in size as it commences filter-feeding, although initial growth increments remain modest during the first several months post-settlement.

As individuals progress through the juvenile bivalve stage, a distinct size threshold signals the approach of reproductive maturity. Examination of shell annuli from wild populations indicates that Tritogonia verrucosa attains a shell length at puberty of approximately 6 cm [Lp = approximately 6 cm], corresponding to an age of roughly 20 years based on growth curve estimates. This delayed maturation is consistent with the slow life-history strategy observed among many unionid mussels inhabiting stable lotic environments. Once puberty is reached, the sexually mature adult allocates resources toward gametogenesis and subsequent spawning events. The reproductively active adult can achieve a remarkable ultimate shell length of 11.7 cm [Li = 11.7 cm] under favorable conditions, making it one of the larger members of its genus. Long-term mark-recapture studies have documented individuals attaining this ultimate shell length only after many decades of continuous growth, reflecting the species' exceptionally low metabolic turnover and extended lifespan.

Body mass scaling in Tritogonia verrucosa follows a predictable allometric relationship relative to shell dimensions. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is estimated at 57.6 grams [Wwi = 57.6 grams], a value derived from size-corrected data for a related species, Unio tumidus. This corresponds to a robust body mass for a bivalve of 11.7 cm shell length, reflecting the thick, heavily sculptured valves characteristic of this species. The relationship between shell length and tissue mass is influenced by both age and local environmental conditions, with individuals from nutrient-rich rivers tending to achieve higher condition indices. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the growth coefficient is relatively low, contributing to the extended period required to reach asymptotic size. Seasonal variation in wet weight occurs as glycogen reserves are mobilized for gamete production during the spring spawning period, with a subsequent recovery phase during the summer feeding months.

Longevity data for Tritogonia verrucosa indicate one of the most extended lifespans recorded among North American freshwater mussels. Under natural conditions, the life span is typically 12 years [am = 12 years] at a water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], although earlier reports by Bauer in 1987 documented individuals reaching 93 years in undisturbed habitats. This exceptional longevity is facilitated by a slow metabolic rate, low predation pressure in the silt and gravel substrates of large rivers, and a conservative reproductive strategy that spreads reproductive effort over many decades. The natural death of senescent individuals occurs gradually, with growth rings becoming increasingly compressed near the shell margin during the final years of life. Habitat degradation and the introduction of invasive species such as Dreissena polymorpha have likely reduced the average lifespan in contemporary populations, although the physiological potential for extreme longevity remains encoded in the species' life-history template.
